verdict: Avoid new readymade-garments exposure in Okhla until Delhi demand and national garment output turn; only lend to domestic-focused, low-leverage converters with tight monthly structure.
title: Okhla Readymade Garments & Made-ups: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Okhla garment units cut, stitch and finish fabric into shirts, trousers and made-ups, then sell to domestic wholesalers, distributors and some exporters. Cash turns on fabric purchase, cutting, stitching, finishing and dispatch; value sits in the order book and finished-goods inventory, not in the machines. **The cost stack is fabric plus labour plus power, and pricing power is thin because buyers can shift orders.** Working capital is inventory-heavy and receivables run long, so the cycle, not the margin, decides survival.

## What has changed now
Delhi's own demand is lagging: GST collections are +2.7% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, 3.4 pp slower [D], and electricity demand is +6.5% against India's +9.5%, 3.0 pp slower [D]. Nationally, garment output (NIC 14) is -7.4% YoY and -5.6% Apr-to-date [D]. **The data-based call is AVOID, and the local and national signals both point the same way.** Peer results are mixed: Raymond Lifestyle's garmenting order book runs to mid-Feb'27 but cost pressure dented 2Q [4]; Sangam's Q4 FY26 net profit fell to Rs.4.3 Cr from Rs.12.8 Cr [5]; KKCL sees festive volume growth but discretionary softness [6]. Local Okhla-specific coverage is thin; the directory listings [1][2][3] give contacts, not financials.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue domestic-focused converters with confirmed wholesale orders and no export dependence.** The peer read is that garmenting scale-up and festive domestic demand are the live drivers [4][6], while export-linked names face end-market moderation [10]. Avoid pure export job-workers and units whose order book is verbal. When a proposal lands, check the buyer mix and the order book; if more than half is export or unconfirmed, ask for signed purchase orders and last twelve months' buyer-wise sales.

## How to grow safely
**Structure short: cash credit against paid stock and book debts, with a drawing power recalculated monthly.** Take stock and debtor statements every month, plus GST returns and bank statements. Set a covenant that inventory days and receivable days stay within agreed limits; if either slips, ask for the ageing and the top-five buyer list. Cap total exposure per unit and keep tenor to one season.

## Early-warning signs
- **GST turnover falling below the sanctioned drawing power (monthly):** cut limits and ask for the sales register. - **Receivable days stretching beyond the agreed cap (monthly):** ask for buyer-wise ageing and stop fresh disbursal. - **Finished-goods stock rising while sales fall (monthly):** inspect godown and revalue drawing power. - **Power or wage arrears appearing in bank statements (monthly):** treat as a cash-flow break and review the account.
